title: Scope, time & cost
examples: How does changing the scope affect the timeline?
What is the relationship between cost and time in a project?
Can we increase the scope without increasing the budget?

explain.say: Today we discuss the project triangle concept.
These three elements form a critical balance in any project.
If you change one element, you must adjust at least one other.
Scope creep happens when the project requirements grow without control.
For example, adding a new feature increases both time and cost.

draw.text: New feature = more time and money.

explain.say: In daily life, planning a party shows this triangle clearly.

faq.q: What is the definition of scope creep in project management?
faq.a: Scope creep is the uncontrolled addition of features or requirements to a project. This happens after the project scope has already been agreed upon.
asks: What happens if the scope grows?
Why is uncontrolled scope growth bad?
Can scope creep ruin a project?

faq.q: If we must finish faster, what usually changes?
faq.a: If you reduce the time, you typically must either reduce the scope or increase the cost to compensate.
asks: How does time affect the other two parts?
If time is cut, what gives way?

faq.q: Does increasing the budget always solve scope issues?
faq.a: Increasing the budget gives you more flexibility, but it does not eliminate the need to manage scope changes formally.
asks: How does budget relate to scope creep?

faq.q: What is the most important element to control first?
faq.a: It is crucial to define and freeze the scope as early as possible to maintain control over time and cost.
asks: Which element should we fix first?
How do we lock down the scope?

faq.q: Are there any exceptions to the triangle rule?
faq.a: While the relationship is generally true, complex projects sometimes require specialized risk management to balance these factors.
asks: Are there any exceptions to this rule?
Can we change scope without affecting time?

facts: The project triangle links scope, time, and cost.
Scope creep is uncontrolled expansion of project requirements.
Changing one element requires adjusting at least one other.
A clear scope definition is the first step in planning.

quiz.say: A team decides to add a complex reporting module to an existing software build. This is an example of:
quiz.why: Scope creep is the uncontrolled addition of requirements after the initial agreement.

wrong.0: This only describes the budget aspect, not the source of the problem.
wrong.1: This is the final state, not the process of adding work.
wrong.3: This refers only to the deadline, not the features themselves.

quiz.say: If a client insists on a higher quality finish, they are likely demanding more:
quiz.why: Higher quality generally requires more resources, thus increasing the cost.

wrong.0: While quality might take time, the primary driver for higher quality is usually budget.
wrong.1: Scope refers to what is built, not how well it is built.
wrong.2: Risk is a possibility, not the direct element being increased.

quiz.say: To meet a tight deadline without increasing the budget, the team must most likely:
quiz.why: If time and cost are fixed, the only variable left to adjust is the scope.

wrong.1: This violates the condition that the budget must remain fixed.
wrong.2: This violates the condition that the deadline is tight.
wrong.3: While process improvement helps, it cannot eliminate the need to reduce scope if both time and cost are fixed.
